title: The Complete Cottage Opening Checklist for Georgian Bay Homeowners
seoTitle: Cottage Opening Checklist for Georgian Bay Homeowners
seoDescription: A spring walkthrough for opening your cottage after a Simcoe County winter: exterior, plumbing, electrical, mechanical and interior checks.
html:
Opening your cottage in the spring is one of those tasks that feels straightforward until you actually get out there. Between checking the plumbing after a hard freeze, inspecting the roof, and making sure pests haven't moved in over the winter, there's a lot to cover. Doing it systematically saves you from expensive surprises mid-summer.

Here in the Georgian Bay and Simcoe County region, our winters are hard on structures. Temperature swings, freeze-thaw cycles, and heavy snow loads all take their toll. A methodical opening means you catch issues early, before they turn into costly emergency repairs during peak cottage season. A thorough fall closing makes this process far smoother — see our cottage closing checklist to understand what a proper winterization covers.

Start Outside: Walk the Perimeter First

Before you even unlock the door, do a slow walk around the exterior. Look for frost heaving around the foundation, missing or cracked caulk around windows, damaged fascia or soffits, and any signs of critter entry points. Check the deck boards for any movement, rot, or lifted fasteners — these are trip hazards that should be addressed immediately.

Inspect the roof from the ground (binoculars are handy). Look for missing shingles, lifted flashing around the chimney or vents, and debris buildup in valleys and gutters. Ice damming often leaves clues even after it's thawed — stained ceilings inside are the giveaway.

Plumbing: The Most Critical System

If you winterized your plumbing properly last fall, opening it up is mostly a matter of turning the water back on slowly and checking each fixture for leaks. Do this methodically, one zone at a time. Look under sinks, check toilet connections, and inspect the water heater before firing it back up.

If there was any doubt about whether the system was fully drained or insulated properly, turn the water on cautiously with someone standing near the shut-off valve. A small, slow leak is much better than a burst pipe flooding an interior wall.

Electrical and Mechanical Systems

Check your breaker panel before restoring power to circuits that were off all winter. Look for any signs of moisture intrusion near the panel. Test smoke and carbon monoxide detectors and replace batteries if needed — this is non-negotiable.

For propane or natural gas appliances, smell-test carefully when you first open the structure. If there's any sulphur odour, don't switch anything on — ventilate and call your gas supplier. Inspect the propane tank connections, furnace, and water heater pilot lights before relying on them.

Interior: Mould, Pests, and Settling

Open all windows and doors to air the place out thoroughly before spending any time inside. Check corners, under sinks, and in closets for mould or mildew growth — especially if the property wasn't heated during winter. A dehumidifier running for 24 hours after opening does a lot of good.

Look for signs of rodent activity — droppings, chewed materials, nesting in corners. Mice can cause serious damage to wiring and insulation. If you find evidence of infestation, address it before putting the cottage back into regular use.

Finally, check all door and window hardware. Winter settling often throws hinges out of alignment. A few minutes with a screwdriver and a plane usually solves sticking doors before they become a seasonal annoyance.
